summaries.summary: In 42 BC, Cicero highlighted conversational skills for politics and education, including knowing when and what to discuss and avoiding self-talk.
Conversational norms may become dynamic social conventions shaped by context, culture and language, with online practices evolving faster and little school or linguistic research.
Since Alan Turing's 1950 test, Conversational Systems sought human-like responses, but this paper focuses on NDS that improve usability and user satisfaction by imitating human behavior.
Chatbots are increasingly used for practical purposes, with Facebook Messenger's 900-million-user app, Google's messaging service, and more than 2 billion mobile app users noted.
China leads chatbot adoption through WeChat, released in 2011 by Tecent and used by more than 700 million people, combining multimedia services, bots and human agents.
Existing chatbot engines poorly handle group chats with many users and chatbots, motivating MPCS and three contributions focused on coordination and mediation rather than MPCS norms.
The last section presents some discussion and future work.
Conversation follows social conventions, and social interaction informs, contexts, creates, ratifies, refutes and ascribes power, class, gender, ethnicity and culture through emergent norms.

Designers apply everyday conversational conventions and patterns to meet user expectations, using BIBREF8's implicit interaction framework to distinguish explicit input and output from implicit interactions.

Turn-by-turn social practices manage turn distribution, size and content, while machines struggle with context and dialogue changes, especially with multiple conversational agents and initiative types.

System-initiative systems restrict options with direct questions, user-initiative systems allow freedom and frustration, and mixed-initiative systems face interruptions, human utterances and unclear non-goal-oriented sentences.
Table TABREF5 shows system initiative in question and answer mode, Table TABREF7 shows natural dialogue with shared initiative, and adding another user creates other challenges.
In Table TABREF12, S1 does not reply to certain user utterances, later invites expert chatbots, and S3 alone replies about investing after U2 and U1 agree.
Table TABREF12 illustrates that chatbots need contextual knowledge of when to reply, and MPCS chatbots should fulfill four dimensions of understanding and replying.
The next section presents the state of the art and how they fulfill some of these dimensions.
This section discusses conversational systems by types of interactions, types of architecture, and types of context reasoning, then presents a consolidating comparison table.
Joseph Weizenbaum created ELIZA at the MIT in 1966 to address five fundamental technical problems and reflect patient statements like a psychotherapist.
Kenneth Colby developed PARRY in the early 1970s using MLISP on WAITS and DEC PDP-10, and psychiatrists identified it correctly only 48 percent of the time.
A.L.I.C.E. appeared in 1995, uses AIML, has more than 40,000 categories of knowledge versus ELIZA's about 200, and cannot pass the Turing test.
Cleverbot, developed by Rollo Carpenter, passed the 2011 Turing Test, with Cleverbot voted 59.3 per cent human and humans rated 63.3 per cent human.

Everyday life includes many multi-user conversations, and social media platforms and messaging systems such as WhatsApp expanded asynchronous text conversations in the first 15 years of the 21st century.
Early 2010s advances, including IBM Watson's Jeopardy victory, spurred text-based chatbots and spoken interfaces, but deployments were mostly dyadic dialog between one chatbot and one user.
Dyadic Chatbot.
A Dyadic Chatbot always handles received utterances, works with two members or name mentions, lacks coordination with many members, and includes most chatbots from ELIZA onward.
Multiparty Conversations.
In multiparty conversations, natural language becomes a communication protocol among human users and bots, making a universal computer protocol feasible when every actor engages effectively.
A chief difference between dyadic and multiparty conversations is turn-taking, with some social settings having explicit norms about who speaks, when, and for how long.
Multiparty chatbot creation combines chatbot research and multi-agent coordination research, but lacks solutions for multiparty-aware chatbots or governed chatbots that could increase system trust.
Multi-Dyadic Chatbots.

Sacks et al. found that multiparty spoken conversation generally avoids overlap and uses transition-relevance places, selected-next-speaker cues, first-starter preference, or current-speaker continuation.
A key challenge is determining whether context has determined the next speaker, with vocatives and a bias toward the speaker before the current speaker.
For textual multiparty chatbots, posting determines transition-relevance places, so the main problem is identifying the selected-next-speaker, with no known textual turn-taking modeling work.
Coordination of Multi-Agent Systems.
A multi-agent system is a computational environment where software agents interact cooperatively, competitively or autonomously, access resources and services, and form a complex system.

Multi-agent coordination research uses structured formalized messages, while chatbot coordination regulates social interactions rather than lower-level synchronization, activities and information exchange.
Open multi-agent systems lack centralized control and require law-governed architecture to ensure interactions follow specifications and agents obey the specified scenario.
Minsky introduced laws in 1987 and Law-Governed Interaction, whose low-level distributed-system abstractions lack ability to express high-level social-system information.
Electronic Institution supports interaction norms through high-level abstractions for specifying laws using agent roles, norms and scenes.

XMLaw and the M-Law framework support law-governed mechanisms by intercepting agent messages, checking compliance, redirecting allowed messages, and enforcing permissions, prohibitions and obligations.
Coordinated Aware Chatbots in a Multiparty Conversation.

Chatbot engines lack research on coordination laws integrated with natural language, and the proposed architecture is claimed as the first supporting coordinated aware chatbots in multiparty conversation.
This section presents one implementation of the conceptual architecture, SABIA, CognIA as its instantiation, and the implementation's accuracy and automated tests.
SABIA was developed on Akka middleware, whose Actor Model features include concurrency, distributed computing, resilience, message-passing, actor life cycle management, and actor lookup.
Each Member of the Chat Group is an Actor extending UntypedActor, while SabiaActorSystem is a singleton initializing memory-heavy parsers and implementing Chat Group behavior.
A singleton initialized with the dependency parsing service URL uses tagUtterance on each utterance arrival and parses the returned JSON Object dependency tree using depth-first search.
SABIA does not support invariants for frame parsing, leaving this task to the instantiated application.
Two intent classifiers can be loaded with trained models for runtime use: the 1-nearest-neighbor (1NN) and the SVM-based classifier.

SABIA implements the Action Classifier assuming a relational database with a data schema implementing Figure FIGREF44's conceptual model, leaving database connection and schema compliance to the application.
SABIA provides partially implemented Action behavior through the Template method design pattern BIBREF46, implementing invariant action execution parts and leaving customization placeholders.
CognIA is an instantiation of Sabia framework where group chats contain multiple users and multiple chatbots, including a mediator for financial investment options.
Table TABREF71 shows mixed-initiative dialogue strategy and a dialogue mediator providing coordination control for Q&A, investment simulations, and opinions.
Table SECREF72 presents Cognia interaction norms, with Trigger, Pre-Conditions, and Behavior columns, including cdbguru and poupancaguru behaviors for CDB and Savings Account mentions.
CognIA's interaction norms are implicit from behavior, not explicitly defined as obligations, permissions, and prohibitions, and their small set required no model checking or conflict verification.

On utterance sent with speech act Query_Calculation, if period or initial amount of investment were not specified, Cognia asks the user the missing information.
On utterance sent with speech act Query_Calculation, if period and initial amount of investment were specified and experts are absent, Cognia invites experts and repeats the utterance.
On utterance sent with speech act Query_Calculation, if period and initial amount of investment were specified and experts are present, Cognia repeats the utterance to experts.
On utterance sent with speech act Query_Calculation, Cognia extracts variables and saves the context.
On utterance sent with speech act Query_Calculation, if experts are in the chat and mentioned, Experts extract information, save in the context, compute calculation and send information.
On utterance sent with speech act Inform_Calculation, if Cognia received all replies, Cognia compares the results and inform comparison.
On utterance sent mentioning a chatbot but having no other text, the chatbot replies How can I help you?
On utterance sent that is not understood and has speech act Question, the chatbot replies I don't know... I can only talk about topic X.
On utterance sent that is not understood and has speech act not Question, the chatbot replies I didn't understand.
On utterance sent with speech act one of { Greetings, Thank, Bye }, All chatbots reply to utterance.
On group chat end, All chatbots leave the chat, and the date and time of the end of chat is registered.
CognIA instantiates SABIA with Mediator, Savings Account, CDB and User Actors as Chat Group Members, a Hub using Socket.io and Node.JS, and Socket Clients forwarding broadcasts.
Intents, actions, factual answers, context and logging data are saved in DashDB, and unanswered queries call Search Finance on Social Media on a separate server.
A small dictionary-based topic classifier identifies whether an utterance refers to finance and whether it refers to CDB or Savings Account.
Dependency parsing supports computing return of investment, replacing fragile regular expressions with a TensorFlow implementation BIBREF47 of a SyntaxNet model for Portuguese.

Utterances like "I would like to invest 10 thousands in 3 years" and "10 in 3 years" become normalized forms with the same intent class.
Rules use a depth-first search algorithm combined with Algorithm UID79 rules, and the parser works only for short texts with one period of time and/or initial amount of investment.

CognIA complements speech act classes with action-specific classes, using Inform_Calculation for computed replies and Query_Calculation for queries, listed in table TABREF81.
With no public dataset for financial intents in Portuguese, an incremental Wizard of Oz approach produced 124 questions, then 37 classes, 415 samples, and 3 to 37 samples per class.
The classification method uses word vectors based on co-occurrence frequency, domain-specific documents, and mean word vectors as feature vectors for standard classifiers.
Domain-specific word vectors used 246,945 documents, comprising 184,001 Twitter posts and 62,949 news articles related to finance.
Tweets were crawled from finance expert blog users, news articles came from tweet links, and the set contained 63,270,124 word occurrences and 97,616 distinct words.
The two-step classifier approach began with 1-nearest-neighbor (1NN), where K is 1, then used Support Vector Machines (SVM) with a Gaussian kernel optimized by grid search.
Intent classes used to train the intent classifier were manually mapped to action classes and dependent entities and features, summarized in Table TABREF85.
Most action classes use SABIA's default behavior, with Greet and Bye implemented using rapport, such as replying "Hi" to "Hi".
Search News, Compute and Ask More are the action classes requiring specific implementation for CognIA.
Search News uses search finance on social media service BIBREF49, BIBREF50 to search indexed Portuguese finance Twitter data and return the highest score, if found.

Ask More makes the mediator request missing investment return variables before redirecting to experts, checking context state using ( EQREF46 ) and ( EQREF57 ) and manually added database dependencies.
Compute is implemented by each expert Chatbot, with the savings account chatbot computing ( EQREF90 ) and the certificate of deposit computing ( EQREF92 ), both estimating in Brazil.
The savings account formula variables are INLINEFORM0 return of investment, INLINEFORM1 initial value, INLINEFORM2 interest rate, and INLINEFORM3 rate base.

The certificate of deposit formula variables include INLINEFORM0 return, INLINEFORM1 initial value, INLINEFORM2 Interbank Deposit rate, INLINEFORM3 ID's percentual payed by the bank varying from 90% to 120%, INLINEFORM4 number of days, and INLINEFORM5 income tax.

Table TABREF95 compares classifiers on the first training set, where 1NN exceeded Logistic Regression and Naïve Bayes, while SVM reached accuracies about 12 percentage points higher under leave-one-out validation.
The training set grew from 37 to 63 classes and 415 to 659 samples, with 2 to 63 samples per class; 1NN accuracy dropped, while SVM accuracy differed by about only 1 percentage point.

The framework supports concurrent simulated users, checks expected responses within a maximum time, collects response times and resource metrics, and is divided into SABIA-side and client-side parts.

The tests provide a sanity test for CognIA and performance analysis of SABIA, enabling validation of correct answers, reasonable response times, computing resource consumption, and debugging of specific features.
CognIA was deployed on IBM Bluemix with specified server resources, two dialogues were built, and tests were repeated until standard deviation was less than 1%.
Test 1 ran both dialogues for one user with a 30 seconds maximum wait, and Mediator, CDBExpert, and SavingsAccountExpert responded all expected responses before the maximum time.
Figure FIGREF101 shows dialogue INLINEFORM0 response times, with CDBExpert answering response 3, Mediator taking longest, expert bots responding similarly, and response 19 reaching 20 seconds.
Test 2 ran dialogue INLINEFORM0 with eight concurrent simulated users, a 240 seconds maximum wait, and Figure FIGREF102 showing median response times with maximum and minimum markers.

With eight users, bots take longer than with one user; CDBExpert takes approximately 5 times longer for response 3, concluding responses take approximately 7.3 times more, and response 9 shows 11.4 times longer.
The article explored challenges of engineering MPCS and presented a hybrid conceptual architecture and its implementation with a finance advisory system.
The architecture is being evolved to support decoupled interaction norms specification, and a multi-party governance service is being developed to enforce exchange of compliant utterances.
A micro-service implementation of SABIA is being explored to increase scalability and performance so thousands of members can join thousands of conversations.

The frame_parsing algorithm extracts and saves period and value, then replaces period with "#dt" and value with "#v" in new_intent.
CognIA complements speech act classes with action-specific classes, using Inform_Calculation for computed replies and Query_Calculation for queries, listed in table TABREF81.
With no public dataset for financial intents in Portuguese, an incremental Wizard of Oz approach produced 124 questions, then 37 classes, 415 samples, and 3 to 37 samples per class.
The classification method uses word vectors based on co-occurrence frequency, domain-specific documents, and mean word vectors as feature vectors for standard classifiers.
Domain-specific word vectors used 246,945 documents, comprising 184,001 Twitter posts and 62,949 news articles related to finance.
Tweets were crawled from finance expert blog users, news articles came from tweet links, and the set contained 63,270,124 word occurrences and 97,616 distinct words.
The two-step classifier approach began with 1-nearest-neighbor (1NN), where K is 1, then used Support Vector Machines (SVM) with a Gaussian kernel optimized by grid search.
Intent classes used to train the intent classifier were manually mapped to action classes and dependent entities and features, summarized in Table TABREF85.
Most action classes use SABIA's default behavior, with Greet and Bye implemented using rapport, such as replying "Hi" to "Hi".
Search News, Compute and Ask More are the action classes requiring specific implementation for CognIA.
Search News uses search finance on social media service BIBREF49, BIBREF50 to search indexed Portuguese finance Twitter data and return the highest score, if found.

Ask More makes the mediator request missing investment return variables before redirecting to experts, checking context state using ( EQREF46 ) and ( EQREF57 ) and manually added database dependencies.
Compute is implemented by each expert Chatbot, with the savings account chatbot computing ( EQREF90 ) and the certificate of deposit computing ( EQREF92 ), both estimating in Brazil.
The savings account formula variables are INLINEFORM0 return of investment, INLINEFORM1 initial value, INLINEFORM2 interest rate, and INLINEFORM3 rate base.

The certificate of deposit formula variables include INLINEFORM0 return, INLINEFORM1 initial value, INLINEFORM2 Interbank Deposit rate, INLINEFORM3 ID's percentual payed by the bank varying from 90% to 120%, INLINEFORM4 number of days, and INLINEFORM5 income tax.

Table TABREF95 compares classifiers on the first training set, where 1NN exceeded Logistic Regression and Naïve Bayes, while SVM reached accuracies about 12 percentage points higher under leave-one-out validation.
The training set grew from 37 to 63 classes and 415 to 659 samples, with 2 to 63 samples per class; 1NN accuracy dropped, while SVM accuracy differed by about only 1 percentage point.

The framework supports concurrent simulated users, checks expected responses within a maximum time, collects response times and resource metrics, and is divided into SABIA-side and client-side parts.

The tests provide a sanity test for CognIA and performance analysis of SABIA, enabling validation of correct answers, reasonable response times, computing resource consumption, and debugging of specific features.
CognIA was deployed on IBM Bluemix with specified server resources, two dialogues were built, and tests were repeated until standard deviation was less than 1%.
Test 1 ran both dialogues for one user with a 30 seconds maximum wait, and Mediator, CDBExpert, and SavingsAccountExpert responded all expected responses before the maximum time.
Figure FIGREF101 shows dialogue INLINEFORM0 response times, with CDBExpert answering response 3, Mediator taking longest, expert bots responding similarly, and response 19 reaching 20 seconds.
Test 2 ran dialogue INLINEFORM0 with eight concurrent simulated users, a 240 seconds maximum wait, and Figure FIGREF102 showing median response times with maximum and minimum markers.

With eight users, bots take longer than with one user; CDBExpert takes approximately 5 times longer for response 3, concluding responses take approximately 7.3 times more, and response 9 shows 11.4 times longer.
The article explored challenges of engineering MPCS and presented a hybrid conceptual architecture and its implementation with a finance advisory system.
The architecture is being evolved to support decoupled interaction norms specification, and a multi-party governance service is being developed to enforce exchange of compliant utterances.
A micro-service implementation of SABIA is being explored to increase scalability and performance so thousands of members can join thousands of conversations.
